paragraphs: Navy test pilot Wally Schirra later described it in his autobiography with a precision that left nothing to interpretation. Lieutenant Commander Edward Feightner, assigned to fly the Cutlass with the Blue Angels in 1951, described a colleague who returned from a test flight, threw his helmet on the ground, and said he quit. The hydraulics failed on Feightner's own demonstration flight at eleven hundred feet — below the minimum ejection altitude. Approximately twenty-eight percent of all Cutlasses built were destroyed in accidents. Four test pilots and twenty-one Navy aviators were killed. It was underpowered, unstable, and unforgiving — and everyone who flew it knew that before takeoff.

James Smith McDonnell, the president of McDonnell Aircraft Corporation, personally wrote to the Navy before production began and warned that the F3H powered by the Westinghouse J40 would be a "disappointingly underpowered combination." The Navy overruled him and ordered the aircraft into production anyway. Between 1952 and 1955, eleven Demons crashed. Four pilots were killed. Time magazine called it a fiasco. Congress opened an investigation. The programme lost a hundred and ninety-two million dollars. McDonnell had been right, the Navy had been wrong, and the men who flew the aircraft had paid for the decision the Navy made when it chose not to listen.

The first jet fighter to see mass service with the Air Force was not what it needed for the war it found itself fighting in Korea. The Republic F-84G was designed for ground attack and escort at medium and high altitude, but early combat revealed an aircraft whose thrust fell short of projections at exactly the altitudes and airspeeds where MiG-15s were operating. The Thunderjet could fight. It just could not fight the MiG-15 on equal terms, and every pilot who flew B-29 escort missions over North Korea in 1951 knew it. Forty-two were lost in combat. The aircraft that was supposed to protect the bombers was outclassed by the interceptors assigned to destroy them.

The first production F-102s could not break the sound barrier. This was not a minor deficiency — it was the entire purpose of the aircraft. The problem was the fuselage shape — engineers had recently established that cross-sections needed to follow a specific distribution to pierce the sound barrier, and Convair had ignored it. The Air Force grounded the programme and sent aircraft back for a complete fuselage redesign. The corrected Delta Dagger eventually reached Mach 1.2. But it had entered service as a supersonic interceptor incapable of supersonic flight, and the men who flew the first production aircraft knew it the first time they pushed the throttle forward and watched the Mach meter stop short of one.

At low airspeeds, the F-100A could kill you without warning. The phenomenon was called inertial coupling — a condition where the aircraft's rotational inertia in pitch and roll exceeded its aerodynamic ability to correct, sending the nose upward uncontrollably in what witnesses on the ground came to call the Sabre Dance. North American's test pilots had documented the tendency before the aircraft entered service. The Air Force accepted it anyway. Between 1954 and 1956, twenty-four F-100As were lost in accidents attributable to the handling problem. The F-100A was grounded and withdrawn. Its pilots had been flying an aircraft that the manufacturer knew was dangerous and the Air Force had put into service regardless.

When the F-94C was delivered, its ejection seat fired downward. In a fighter that operated primarily at high altitude against high-altitude bombers, a downward-firing seat made engineering sense: the pilot would be clear of the tail. At low altitude, it meant being fired into the ground. The F-94C was an all-weather interceptor that regularly flew approaches and departures in conditions where altitude margins were minimal, and the downward seat's safe ejection envelope began at altitudes that a pilot in trouble often did not have. The seat was eventually replaced. The pilots who flew the aircraft before the replacement knew the mathematics of their situation and flew anyway, because that was the assignment.

In the air, the Crusader was exceptional. The problem was the carrier. The Crusader's variable-incidence wing required a high angle of attack on approach, which elevated the nose and blocked the pilot's view of the deck at the moment precision was most critical. The nose gear was fragile and prone to collapse. The approach speed was unforgiving. Former Navy pilot David Tussey described landing it as "damn near impossible." The aircraft earned the nickname the Ensign Killer, not because it killed senior aviators but because the accident rate among young, less experienced pilots on their first carrier deployments was disproportionate and difficult to explain as anything other than the aircraft.

Designed to intercept Soviet bombers before they reached American cities, In service it had a secondary tendency to destroy itself. The J35 engines were prone to compressor stalls that could cascade into uncontrollable engine fires. The aircraft's structural design generated resonance problems at certain power settings that maintenance crews documented repeatedly without resolution. Four civilians were killed. The Air Force investigation cited both structural fatigue and engine failure as contributing factors. The F-89 flew for over a decade, accumulating a loss record that its crews understood was not principally the result of enemy action but of the aircraft itself behaving in ways that should have been corrected before it entered operational service.

The British-built Armstrong Siddeley Sapphire licensed as the J65 provided more thrust than the original Thunderjet's J35, but suffered from compressor instability that produced flameouts at altitude. Pilots assigned to nuclear strike missions in Europe, who would fly single-ship profiles at low level and high speed, understood that an engine failure over denied territory was not an emergency with a good resolution. The F-84F accumulated a loss rate that was high enough to generate Congressional scrutiny in 1956. Deliveries were temporarily suspended. The aircraft that NATO's nuclear strike mission depended on was grounded while the Air Force tried to explain why pilots were dying over West Germany before they ever flew toward the enemy.

Korea introduced the F-80 to a war it had not been designed for. The aircraft had been designed as a high-altitude interceptor for European skies and found itself flying ground attack missions at low altitude over terrain that gave defending anti-aircraft crews ideal engagement envelopes. Thirty-two F-80s were lost in the first months of the war. Against the MiG-15 it had no realistic answer — slower, less agile, fighting at altitudes where the Soviet engine performed better than the American one. The F-80's pilots were not flying an aircraft that failed them. They were flying an aircraft that was right for a war that had ended, in a conflict that required something it was not.

In 1965, the finest tactical strike aircraft the Air Force possessed was the F-105D. It was fast, capable of delivering nuclear or conventional weapons, and could sustain supersonic speeds at low altitude that no other aircraft in the inventory matched. Over North Vietnam, none of that mattered as much as the route to the target. Strike packages flew the same corridors repeatedly because the aircraft's range limited their options, and the North Vietnamese built their air defence around those corridors. One F-105 pilot later recalled it plainly: we were going in knowing some of us weren't coming back. The aircraft worked. The mission it was assigned to did not forgive what the aircraft could not change.

The F-4B entered combat without a gun. This was not an oversight. The first engagements over Vietnam revealed that the missiles were not sufficient. The AIM-7 Sparrow had a minimum engagement range that prevented firing in the close manoeuvring combat that actually occurred. The AIM-9 Sidewinder required heat signatures that afterburning MiGs often could not provide in time. Pilots who had trained for beyond-visual-range engagements found themselves in turning fights where the gun they had not been given would have been decisive. The Phantom was added a gun in later variants. The pilots who flew the B model had already learned what doctrine could not protect them from.

Over Vietnam it was asked to turn, to loiter, to engage at low altitude against aircraft that were slower but far more manoeuvrable in the regimes where combat actually occurred. The F-104C's small wing gave it exceptional supersonic performance and extremely poor low-speed handling. The aircraft that could not be beaten above forty thousand feet was poorly suited to the war being fought below ten thousand. The deployment lasted two years. The Air Force quietly withdrew the Starfighter from Southeast Asia and never returned it. The aircraft had not failed. The war had simply required something the aircraft could not provide.

The Air Force transferred the airframes to Tactical Air Command, whose pilots found themselves with an aircraft optimised for straight-line speed and radius of action rather than the manoeuvring combat TAC actually required. The F-101A had no ejection seat upgrade path that addressed its known limitations at high angles of attack. It was large, fast, and difficult to recover from departure — characteristics that had been acceptable in a bomber escort and were considerably less acceptable in a fighter that might need to turn. The aircraft served until attrition and the arrival of the F-105 reduced the requirement. Its pilots flew it knowing it was the wrong tool for what they were being asked to do.

Both roles required the variable-sweep wing — and the wing made the aircraft heavy, too heavy for carrier operations, which the Navy recognised early and the Air Force eventually accepted. The cause was never fully established. The programme was suspended, the aircraft withdrawn, and a lengthy investigation produced recommendations that required structural modifications to address fatigue cracking that should have been identified before the aircraft flew operationally. The F-111 eventually became a capable strike platform. The early versions that went to Vietnam were not that aircraft. Three were lost in the first six weeks. The Air Force had sent them anyway.

Captain Lee Tillotson, the Navy's F-14 programme coordinator, was more specific: from the very start, he said, you essentially teach the pilots to fly the engine as a priority over flying the airplane. The problem was compressor stalls at high angles of attack — the exact manoeuvre that air combat required. One former F-14 pilot later described losing both engines during a routine engagement: in an F-4, he wrote, the engines would have been fine. Thirty-six F-14As were lost to causes attributable to the TF30. The Navy had known before deployment. No better engine was available on the schedule the programme required. So they sent the one they had.

In name it was a Sabre. Fighter pilots assigned to the D model received an aircraft that had removed their judgment from the most critical moment of the engagement. The radar and fire control system required constant precise inputs under conditions that cockpit workload made difficult to maintain. The single-pilot workload in instrument conditions, conducting an intercept, managing the fire control system, and flying the aircraft simultaneously, was documented as excessive by Air Defense Command's own assessors. The pilots who had come from dogfighters found themselves managing a system that had decided the pilot was the least reliable component in the engagement.

Navy night fighter pilots had a name for the Douglas F3D-2. They called it Drut. It was, as its nickname implied, a blunt assessment of what it was like to fly. The aircraft had accumulated a reasonable night interception record against propeller-driven aircraft. Against jets it was outmatched in every performance parameter. The crews who flew it in Korea were aware that if they were detected, they could not evade. The J34 engines provided thrust adequate for the aircraft's original design weight and substantially less adequate for the combat configuration that operational requirements had added to it. Its crews flew with the knowledge that escape was not among the options the aircraft provided.

The pilot managed the systems, monitored the aircraft, and ejected if something went wrong. Air Defense Command pilots who had trained as fighter pilots found themselves in an aircraft where their instincts and judgement had been replaced by a ground computer that neither knew nor cared what the pilot saw through the canopy. Some described it as flying a very expensive bus that happened to go Mach two. The SAGE system was doctrinally sound for the long-range bomber interception mission. The men assigned to fly it were fighter pilots who had not been trained to be bus drivers and never entirely forgave the Air Force for making them one.

The J71 provided more thrust than the J40 had delivered in practice, but still fell short of what a carrier fighter of the Demon's weight required. Pilots who flew the F3H-2 described an aircraft that was stable and capable within its limits, but whose limits were narrower than the mission demanded. The aircraft never shook the reputation the J40 programme had built for it. Squadrons that had watched colleagues die in J40-powered airframes brought institutional memory to their J71 conversions that no maintenance bulletin could address. The Demon served from 1956 to 1964 — eight years of adequate performance in an aircraft that had spent its entire existence being trusted less than it deserved and more than was entirely safe.

It was also already obsolete before the first production aircraft was delivered. The aircraft that entered service with demonstration teams and fleet squadrons was excellent at the mission it had been built for and inadequate for the mission the fleet actually needed. In 1956 test pilot Tom Attridge fired the Tiger's own twenty-millimetre cannon during a firing run and flew through his own shells, damaging his own aircraft — a demonstration that the aircraft was faster than its own weapons. It was replaced by the Crusader and the Phantom. The Tiger had arrived perfectly, for a navy that no longer existed.

The weapons system operator had no flight controls. McDonnell had designed the aircraft to weight and performance specifications that left no room for duplicate controls, and Air Defense Command had accepted the limitation because the mission — nuclear-armed intercept of high-altitude bombers — did not contemplate survival scenarios of that kind. The operators who flew the back seat of the F-101B flew an aircraft where their fate was entirely in the hands of someone else, with no recourse if that someone else became unable to perform. They flew it anyway, for a decade, because someone had decided the design constraint was acceptable.

Built for export, the F-5 was inexpensive and simple — qualities the Air Force did not value. American pilots assigned to Vietnam found themselves in an aircraft that had been designed for export economies rather than the operational requirements of the USAF. It was underpowered compared to what they had trained on, limited in range, and carried a weapons load that the missions often demanded more of than the aircraft could provide. The pilots who flew it professionally did so competently. The pilots who had come from F-100s and F-105s and been assigned an export fighter because the situation required it were flying an aircraft they had not chosen and did not trust in the margins where trust mattered most.

Five days on a carrier proved what years of engineering had not resolved. The Navy received the aircraft, flew it from USS Coral Sea on trials, and rejected it. The aircraft was too heavy for carrier operations by a margin that Grumman's engineers could not design away. Its empty weight exceeded the carrier approach speed limitations that the deck equipment could handle. The Navy cancelled the programme and began the design work that would produce the F-14. The F-111B's test pilots had flown an aircraft that the service had commissioned, funded, tested, and then concluded was simply not a carrier aircraft. The war for which it had been designed did not wait for the replacement to arrive.

paragraphs: On the fourteenth of August 1945, Japan announced its surrender. Within a week, the United States Navy cancelled construction contracts on thirty-two destroyers sitting on the ways at shipyards from Bath to Pascagoula. Steel already cut. Keels already laid. Workers who had been building warships at the pace the Pacific demanded were told to stop. The Gearing and Sumner hulls that would never be finished represented the last expression of a destroyer concept that had proved itself across four years of Pacific combat — fast, well-armed, adaptable, and present in numbers that mattered. The war ended before the Navy had to ask what came next. The answer turned out to be harder than anyone expected.

The first question the postwar Navy tried to answer was not what the next destroyer would be, but whether destroyers and escorts needed to remain separate categories at all. SCB-7 was the attempt — a thirty-knot destroyer leader that could keep station with carrier task forces while still performing the antisubmarine mission that slower convoy escorts had handled during the war. It grew too large and too expensive before it reached production, absorbed into the thinking that eventually produced the Norfolk and the Mitscher. The postwar Navy needed to decide what it was building against. It would spend the next decade discovering that the threat was moving faster than the answer.

USS Norfolk was built as a hunter-killer — a ship specifically designed to find and destroy the fast Soviet submarines that German Type XXI technology had made possible. She was large, expensive, and genuinely capable of the mission she was given. One was built. The follow-on series was cancelled. The Navy's conclusion was that a ship optimised for a single mission in an era of multiplying threats was a resource allocation the fleet could not sustain. Norfolk's design informed the Mitscher class and then disappeared into the broader debate about what surface combatants actually needed to do. The postwar Navy had built its first specialised ASW destroyer leader. It then decided that specialisation itself was the problem.

The Typhon system was supposed to change everything about surface warfare — engaging aircraft, missiles, and submarines simultaneously at ranges no previous shipborne system had approached. The nuclear hull was projected to cost more than the combined budget of the other destroyer programmes competing for the same appropriation. Robert McNamara cancelled Typhon in November 1962, along with the nuclear-powered destroyer that would have carried it into service. The system that might have defined Cold War surface warfare for a generation was terminated simultaneously with the propulsion philosophy that was the only practical way to operate it.

Nuclear propulsion was not experimental. By 1963, the Navy wanted it to be standard. The Chief of Naval Operations agreed: a formal proposal went to the Secretary of Defense calling for nuclear propulsion to become the baseline for all new major surface combatants, including destroyers. The logic was sound — unlimited range, no refuelling vulnerability, sustained high-speed operations. McNamara rejected it on cost grounds — not after debate, but as a decision already made. The Navy had asked whether nuclear destroyers were better. McNamara's answer was that better and affordable were not the same question, and that the question he was answering was the second one.

Congress authorised the nuclear Strike Cruiser in 1978 with enough funding to begin detailed design. President Carter vetoed the appropriation. Congress reauthorised it. Carter vetoed it again. The CSGN was a ship that the Navy wanted, the shipbuilding industry wanted, and the legislative branch twice approved — cancelled not by cost overruns or performance failures but by a president who had decided that nuclear surface ships were the wrong strategic investment at a moment when the Navy's argument for them was stronger than it had ever been. The Strike Cruiser would have been the most capable surface combatant ever built by any navy. It was never laid down because one man with veto authority disagreed.

Fifty ships. That was the original plan — that would give the Navy a modern antisubmarine force in one coordinated procurement cycle. Congress approved thirty. The Reagan administration's five-year plan included six more in the FY1986–87 budget. None were built. The Spruance class that entered service was already a compromise: the right hull, the right propulsion, the right sensors, built in numbers that made the replacement problem permanent rather than solving it. The Navy's plan had been to field a generation. What it got was the basis for the next argument about what came after.

Iran ordered six advanced Spruance variants with full area air defence capability in 1973. When the Shah fell in 1979, four completed ships came to the US Navy as the Kidd class — immediately recognised as more capable general-purpose warships than the standard Spruances alongside them. The logical conclusion was to upgrade the entire thirty-one-ship class to the same standard. The cost of doing so across a class that size was calculated, presented, and declined. The Kidds became the most capable destroyers the US Navy operated in the 1980s. The ships they were based on were retired without ever receiving what the Iranians had paid for.

The Navy examined this possibility seriously in 1976 — a destroyer-sized ship capable of operating VSTOL aircraft and ASW helicopters simultaneously, combining the Spruance's submarine-hunting capability with limited organic air power in a single platform. The concept was sound in principle and prohibitive in practice: a ship modified to carry fixed-wing aircraft could not simultaneously optimise its sonar systems, and a ship optimised for ASW could not provide the deck space that meaningful VSTOL operations required. The Navy was no longer designing destroyers for what they needed to do. It was testing competing ideas on the same hull and hoping the hull was large enough to accommodate them all.

Designed for a destroyer. Redesignated a cruiser before the keel was laid. DDG-47 — Ticonderoga — had been programmed as a guided missile destroyer in the standard hull-number sequence, intended to demonstrate that Aegis could fit within destroyer constraints. When the cost and capability of the final design became clear, the Navy reclassified it as a cruiser to reflect what it had actually built. The destroyer that was supposed to democratise Aegis became instead the expensive baseline that Aegis destroyers would eventually need to replace. The move that was intended to show restraint produced a twenty-seven-ship cruiser class instead of a larger, cheaper destroyer programme.

If Aegis was too expensive for standard destroyer procurement, the question was whether a simplified version of the system could fit a modified Spruance hull at a cost the fleet could sustain in numbers. The 1982 study examined exactly this — a modified Spruance hull carrying a reduced-capability Aegis suite that would provide area air defence without the full cruiser price. The Navy needed a purpose-built Aegis destroyer, which eventually became the Arleigh Burke. What the austere studies demonstrated was that compromising the system to fit the hull was the same mistake as building the full system on the wrong hull. The answer had to be a new ship.

Seventy-five hulls. That was the Cold War plan — a force large enough to replace the retiring Spruances and Adams-class ships while sustaining carrier and amphibious group escort requirements simultaneously. The Soviet Union collapsed as the first Burkes were commissioning. The procurement rate that had justified the eighty-ship figure was recalculated against a threat that no longer existed at the scale that had produced the requirement. The Burke that was designed as the mass-produced answer to Soviet naval power became instead the only destroyer the Navy could afford to keep building — which turned out to be a different kind of indispensability.

Five hundred vertical launch cells. Fifty sailors. No sensors or combat systems to target its own weapons — directed entirely by data from other platforms in the network. The unit cost was projected at less than half a Burke. A competitive programme was initiated in 1996, four design teams submitted proposals, and the contract was cancelled in 1997 before a prototype was awarded. The concept violated the institutional logic of surface warfare — a ship that cannot fight for itself is not a warship — and that logic proved more durable than the strategic argument for building one.

Fewer than twenty-five years in service. The Navy retired all thirty-one anyway. The Ticonderoga cruisers — built on the same hull and powered by the same machinery — received a service life extension in 2003 that kept them operational for thirty-five years. The Spruances did not receive that investment. Not one was preserved as a museum ship. The destroyer class that had introduced gas turbine propulsion to the US Navy, that had fired more Tomahawk missiles in Desert Storm than any other platform, was decommissioned in its entirety while ships it had influenced were still being built. It was the right ship for the wrong decade.

It was called DD-21 — destroyer for the twenty-first century. When the requirement was restructured in 2001 it became DD(X). When a hull number was assigned in 2006 it became DDG-1000. At each renaming the planned quantity fell: thirty-two to twenty-four to seven. The reason was identical at every stage — cost per hull rising as the total procurement shrank, producing a spiral in which each reduction made the programme more expensive, which caused the next reduction. A programme designed to procure a class affordable enough to replace an entire generation of destroyers became the most expensive destroyer programme in US Navy history, measured per hull.

Twenty-nine ships were not built. Three were. DDG-1000 was designed around two Advanced Gun Systems firing a rocket-assisted guided projectile that would give the fleet naval gunfire support at ranges previously requiring air strikes. The primary mission the ship had been designed to perform was eliminated. DDG-1000's tumblehome hull, integrated electric drive, and reduced radar signature were genuine engineering achievements — applied to a platform that had lost its reason for existing before the third hull was commissioned. The guns were removed. Hypersonic missiles were installed. The destroyer built to support troops ashore became a platform for weapons that will never fire at a beach.

Every Ticonderoga that decommissions leaves a gap. CG(X) was supposed to close it — providing area air defence and ballistic missile defence to carrier strike groups whose dedicated cruiser coverage was running out. A cruiser-sized hull carrying advanced radar, large numbers of interceptor missiles, and a power plant capable of directing-energy weapons was the stated requirement. The programme was cancelled in the first Obama administration budget in 2010, replaced by the decision to procure additional Flight III Arleigh Burke destroyers with improved Aegis capability. The fleet's cruiser replacement became a destroyer upgrade. The capability gap that CG(X) was intended to close remains open. Every Ticonderoga that decommissions makes it wider.

Not a ship. A system. an integrated surface action group consisting of DD-21 destroyers, CG-21 cruisers, and Arsenal Ships operating as a networked strike force that would project power from the sea without requiring carrier aviation. The three components were designed together, validated together, and cancelled together when the Future Surface Combatant Programme restructured the requirement in 2001. What survived was DD(X) alone, stripped of the cruiser and arsenal components that had given the original concept its strategic logic. The Navy had briefly imagined a surface force capable of independent power projection. What it built instead were three destroyers whose primary armament had no ammunition.

Four years. No Burkes. The procurement pause was deliberate — the DDG-1000 programme was absorbing the shipbuilding funds that would otherwise have sustained Burke production, and the Navy believed it was transitioning to a superior class. During those four years the fleet continued retiring older destroyers and cruisers on schedule. The gap between ships leaving the inventory and ships entering it widened. When the Navy reversed course in 2010 and restarted Burke procurement, it was acknowledging that the transition had failed — but the force structure damage done during the pause could not be recovered on the timelines the budget permitted.

Mission modules. The promise was that one hull could become any ship the Navy needed. would allow it to be reconfigured as the threat required — a single hull performing antisubmarine, surface warfare, or mine countermeasure missions by swapping out equipment packages. The modules were developed in parallel with the ships, fell behind schedule, exceeded cost estimates, and in most cases never achieved the operational capability the concept required. Two different hull designs were built in parallel. Neither achieved the mission flexibility that had justified the programme. Modularity sounded like flexibility. In practice, it meant nothing worked.

Ten contracted. Four cancelled before steel was cut. The Constellation class had been selected as a low-risk parent-design adaptation of the Italian FREMM frigate — a proven hull that would avoid the development costs that had destroyed the LCS and DDG-1000 programmes. US Navy requirements added weight, changed systems, and drove a redesign that increased the ship's displacement by thirteen percent before the first hull was delivered. The first delivery slipped from 2026 to 2029. The Navy cancelled four contracted hulls and accelerated delivery of the two already under construction. A programme justified as low-risk had produced the same cost and schedule outcome as every high-risk programme it was designed to avoid.

In 2021, the Navy established a programme to replace both the Burke and the Ticonderoga. — a single large surface combatant that would carry more power, more missiles, and more growth margin than the Burke design could accommodate. In December 2025 the programme was cancelled and replaced with an announcement of a new battleship class. Whether the battleship will be funded, designed, or built remains unresolved. The United States Navy has been trying to replace the Arleigh Burke for thirty years. The Burke is still in production. The replacement that has been announced most recently has not received a dollar of appropriated funding.

July 2008. The Chief of Naval Operations recommended stopping DDG-1000 at two ships — and that Burke production resume. The recommendation acknowledged that the programme which had been designed to replace the Spruance class had instead produced two hulls at a combined cost that exceeded the total procurement value of the entire thirty-one-ship Spruance class it was meant to replace. The Navy had spent fourteen years and over ten billion dollars in development costs on a destroyer class that would field three ships. It was made because continuing would have consumed the shipbuilding budget of an entire decade for a programme that had already consumed a generation.

Designed in the 1980s. Keel laid in 1988. The lead ship commissioned in 1991. In 2010 — nineteen years after USS Arleigh Burke entered service — the United States Navy restarted production of a design it had stopped building five years earlier because nothing developed in the intervening decade had proven capable of replacing it. The Flight III variant that is currently being procured incorporates thirty years of upgrades onto a hull form that has reached the limit of its growth margin. The question the postwar Navy first asked in 1945 — what should a destroyer be — remains the question it is still asking.
